This is due to this check in Range (`range.cpp`) added by https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/81076: If we remove this check, then non-finite values become allowed.

They have to be typed as `INF`, `-INF`, or `NAN` like GDScript, and then get displayed as `inf`, `-inf`, or `nan`: Inside of the `.tscn` file the values get serialized as `inf`, `inf_neg`, or `nan`: So, it's clear that simply removing this check is not enough.

We need to fix these problems:

* The text the user can type is not the same as the displayed text (vital for good UX).
* The constants in GDScript are not the same as the displayed text (ideal for good UX).
* The value serialized in the file is not the same as the displayed text in the case of `-inf` and `inf_neg` (less important, but we should still be consistent).

Allowing the user to type both `inf` and `INF` is just generally a good idea, and stands on its own, so I put this into a separate PR here: #100395.
This fixes the first point, since users can type `inf` like they see `inf`.\r\n\r\nHowever, I think there is value in fixing the other two points as well.

Capitalizing the displayed and serialized text is pretty straightforward, it's just an arbitrary choice we make as engine developers, although we need to keep the code being able to read `inf` and such to keep reading old files (and if this is merged, we should backport a fix to older branches to allow `INF` etc to be read by older Godot versions).\r\n\r\nAs for `inf_neg`, the current reason for this is that VariantParser is not able to parse `-INF` as a single thing.

### Issue description

I'm not actually sure if this is actually a bug, or just undocumented behavior, so there could be room for discussion.

At least through a quick search in the docs, I can't find any warning that `preload()` is unable to unload resources, and yet, [it is widely recommended as the default option in official docs pages](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3 …

This causes them to be pinned to memory for the entirety of the game's runtime, with no clear warning signs of how bad this can be.\n\nAs a consequence, if a game preloads heavy scenes, such as entire levels, a long session might cause the game to slow down or even crash, due to the continuous pile-up of resources that never get cleaned up by Godot.

That means using `preload()` is as dangerous as creating cyclic references between RefCounted objects, if not more because resources can contain large amounts of data.

Notes:
- This is not a memory leak, because the resources can still be loaded from the cache, so a specific resource won't be instantiated multiple times.
- This seems to be directly caused by #77513, since preloads are held by compiled scripts.
- Despite the similar name, the ResourcePreloader node is not affected by this.
Its resources are held by the scene resource, same as `@export` vars.

### Issue description

When a slider has a negative `min_value` (for some reason this only repros with small negative values like 0.2), and a `value` of 0.0, it behaves correctly in the editor, but when the project is run, the slider initializes to the wrong default value.

Instead of being set to 0.0, it can initialize all the way left, or right, or somewhere else in between, depending on the minimum value.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a slider.
2.
Set its min_value to a small negative (e.g. -0.2).
For some reason, this doesn't work for larger values like -1.0.\n3.
Leave or explicitly set its value to 0.0.\n4.
Optionally: log or display the value of the slider.\n5.

Run the project.

Expected behaviour: the slider's initial value is 0.0 (i.e. not all the way to the left, because of the negative minimum).
Observed behaviour: the slider's initial value is -0.2 (all the way to the left).

Bizarrely, for some minimum values (e.g. -0.5) the slider starts all the way to the right instead.

Notice: In the .tscn file, the "value" is not stored at all, because it is the default of 0.0.

I'm not sure if this is a clue (the slider might assume incorrectly that the default value is not 0.0 but in fact all the way left).

That would probably require saving a version number inside the project (or each resource maybe, to support plugins ?) to check if a resource needs an update.

Even if I didn't touch the scene as part of my workflow, the property is still modified on save.

You can see the values updating live in the editor as well while the tree is running.

For example:

before
```
[node name="Sprite2D" type="Sprite2D" parent="."]
texture = ExtResource("1_5rya8")
hframes = 4
frame = 1
```

after
```
[node name="Sprite2D" type="Sprite2D" parent="."]
texture = ExtResource("1_5rya8")
hframes = 4
frame = 4
```

### Steps to reproduce

Animate a property of some scene via an `AnimationPlayer`.
Connect it to an `AnimationTree`.
Enable the `AnimationTree`.
Save the scene without modifying the `frame` property
Observe that sometimes the scene's `tscn` is modified with a new value for property.
